caption:
“Trusting the experts” is used in religion and despotic authoritarianism, it has no place in science or a free society. There was a day when science hailed cocaine as a wonder anesthetic for toothaches and pain, sold over-the-counter in tonics and lozenges for everything from depression to impotence—until addiction rates exploded (over 200,000 cases in the US by the early 1900s), leading to its ban under the 1914 Harrison Narcotic Act amid reports of hallucinations and dependency.  
  
Heroin followed a parallel path: introduced by Bayer in 1898 as a “non-addictive” alternative to morphine, it was marketed as a cough syrup safe even for children’s colds, with ads depicting spoonfuls for sore throats and claiming it was five times more effective. By the 1910s, its addictive nature became undeniable, prompting Bayer to discontinue it in 1913 and the FDA to ban it in 1924. In the mid-20th century, cigarette smoking was promoted for digestion in 1930s-50s ads, like those for Camels asserting it stimulated digestive fluids and aided alkalinity, with doctors endorsing brands as “healthier” or less irritating—until cancer links emerged in the 1940s, resulting in a 1951 FTC ban on such claims.  
  
Lobotomies, developed in 1936, severed frontal lobe connections through crude methods like ice picks inserted via the eyes, positioned as a quick “fix” for depression and mental agitation based on early neurology. Despite risks including a 15% death rate, relapses, and severe personality changes (as seen in Rosemary Kennedy’s case), it was performed widely until banned by 1967 due to ethical outcries and fatal complications. Finally, electroshock therapy was used from the 1950s-70s as a “conversion” tool for homosexuality, which mainstream medicine considered a mental disorder until the 1970s; often paired with aversion shocks during exposure to same-gender images, it affected thousands in the UK and US and wasn’t discontinued until after the 1973 diagnosis declassification.

Pair carbohydrates with protein, fiber, and healthy fat—and take a 10–15 minute walk after meals when you can.

Aim for consistent, restorative sleep. Your immune system does much of its repair work overnight.

Walking and strength training help improve blood sugar regulation, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory signaling.

Breathwork, meditation, time in nature, meaningful relationships, and real recovery all help calm an overactive stress response.

You don’t have to overhaul your life overnight. Start with one habit. Then another.

There’s a two week window every month where eating the wrong thing can quietly work against your hormones, and most women have never been told about it.

Conventional medicine’s answer to hormone imbalance is usually birth control. It works for some people, but it’s a blanket fix for a problem that’s rarely one size fits all. Seed cycling is a different approach, and it’s simpler than it sounds.

During the follicular phase, the first half of your cycle, your body is building up estrogen. Flaxseed and pumpkin seed support that process through their lignan and zinc content. After ovulation, during the luteal phase, your body shifts to needing progesterone, and that’s where sesame and sunflower seed come in.

This isn’t just a wellness trend with no backing. 

A 2025 systematic review found seed cycling significantly reduced PMS symptoms, including bloating, breast tenderness, and mood swings. Other emerging research has linked it to improved insulin and androgen balance in women with PCOS.

In my telehealth clinic, I always frame this as one piece of a bigger picture. Seed cycling supports hormone production, but if you’re dealing with significant hormone imbalance, it usually needs to sit alongside proper testing and a personalized plan, not replace it.

I walk through the full protocol, which seeds to eat when, and what to do if your cycle isn’t regular in the article.

caption:
That ibuprofen you take for a headache does a lot more inside your body than most people realize.

NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandins, the compounds responsible for pain and inflammation. That sounds like a good thing, and in the short term it is. But prostaglandins also protect your stomach lining, reduce excess stomach acid, and support gut healing. Block them regularly and you lose all of that protection along with the pain relief.

This is how NSAIDs end up linked to long term issues like gut irritation, ulcers, and increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Even occasional use can affect people who already have an existing gut imbalance or inflammatory condition.

I’m not telling you to never take one again. If ibuprofen is the only thing getting you through severe menstrual cramps or helping you sleep through a migraine, the benefit can outweigh the risk in that moment.

There are real alternatives with research behind them. Curcumin, boswellia, and white willow bark all show meaningful pain relief without the same gut disruption. In my telehealth clinic, I use these with patients regularly, especially anyone reaching for NSAIDs more than occasionally.

You could be 40 or 50 years away from knowing whether your habits paid off. Or you could look at your walking pace right now.

A new study followed nearly 4,000 adults in their 80s and found that the fastest walkers, people moving quicker than 93 percent of their peers, were 50 percent less likely to develop cognitive impairment, and 60 percent less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or another dementia. Walking briskly requires your brain, heart, lungs, and nervous system to coordinate in real time. Losing that coordination may be one of the earliest signs your brain is changing.

Luckily gait speed is trainable. Focus on cadence, not just stride. Add short bursts of brisk walking a few times a week. Strengthen your hips and core. Swing your arms.

That’s 46 teaspoons in a single drink.

For perspective, the American Heart Association recommends limiting added sugar to no more than 25 grams (6 teaspoons) per day for women and 36 grams (9 teaspoons) per day for men. 

This one drink contains more than 5 days’ worth of added sugar for most women—and more than 5 times the recommended daily limit for men.

Now imagine drinking 186 grams all at once.

Within minutes, your blood sugar begins to surge. Your pancreas releases a flood of insulin to bring it back down. Your liver is forced to process an enormous fructose load, converting much of the excess into fat and triglycerides. Fat burning is put on hold while your body deals with the overload.

A few hours later, many people experience the crash: fatigue, brain fog, irritability, and cravings for even more sugar as stress hormones rise to stabilize blood sugar.

One drink won’t give you diabetes.

But when products like this become normal—and repeated blood sugar spikes become part of everyday life—they can contribute to insulin resistance, fatty liver disease, chronic inflammation, weight gain, and type 2 diabetes over time.

Your body was never designed to process 46 teaspoons of sugar in one sitting, or even one week… please do not drink this.

This doesn't mean coffee prevents dementia or guarantees protection. This was an observational study, so it can't prove cause and effect. But it adds to growing evidence that the habits we practice consistently over decades can influence brain health as we age.

Your daily habits matter. Sleep. Exercise. Blood sugar control. A nutrient-dense diet. Strong social connections. And yes... your morning cup of coffee may be one small piece of the puzzle. ☕🧠

For years, the assumption has been simple: struggling to focus means you have ADHD, and the fix is medication. But that's not the whole story.

Real ADHD is genetic. It shows up in families, and the underlying issue is a difference in dopamine, the brain chemical responsible for focus and motivation. But there's another category entirely: symptoms that look identical to ADHD but come from your environment. Ultra-processed food. Chronic stress. Notifications pulling at your attention all day. 

None of that requires a diagnosis. It requires a reset.

A randomized controlled trial published in The Lancet tested this directly. Kids with ADHD were put on a strict 5-week elimination diet, and 64 percent showed a significant reduction in symptoms. 

When common trigger foods were reintroduced, many relapsed. 

Before you or your child gets a diagnosis, it's worth ruling out what's fixable. Diet. Sleep. Screen time. If the pattern is truly genetic, it will still be there in a month. If it's your environment, you'll already feel the difference.

There’s a detox protocol built almost entirely around beans, and the story behind it is wilder than you’d expect. It was developed in the early 90s by a biochemist named Karen Hurd, who used it to help her own daughter recover from severe illness related to pesticide exposure.

The idea is soluble fiber. Beans and lentils are loaded with it, and soluble fiber binds to bile that’s carrying toxins and excess hormones, escorting it out of your body through bowel movements instead of letting it recirculate. When that recirculation happens too much, it shows up as fatigue, hormonal imbalance, food sensitivities, and inflammation.

Here’s where I get more cautious than the internet version of this trend. Beans are also high in lectins and phytates, and for people who already have gut imbalances, autoimmunity, or SIBO, eating beans 3 to 6 times a day can make things significantly worse instead of better. The people this protocol is marketed to are often the exact people most likely to react badly to it.

In my telehealth clinic, I don’t recommend this across the board. Bio individuality matters more here than almost anywhere else I see in nutrition.
